paras: The attempted lynching of Joe Edwards took place in St. Louis, Missouri, on the afternoon of September 13, 1881, when a street crowd seized Edwards, a Black steamboat fireman, after he fired a pistol in a quarrel with another Black man and wounded a woman passing by. The crowd held him while men ran for a rope, but police arrived and took him to the station. Telegraph dispatches carried the story to dailies in Texas, Tennessee, Indiana and Minnesota the next day, and Midwestern weeklies reprinted it in their crime roundups.

According to the wire report, Edwards and Al Guffin were 'two negro firemen on the steamer Porter' who had had a difficulty that morning. The Dallas Daily Herald's St. Louis correspondent instead said the two men, whom it called Al. Griffin and Joe Edwards, had quarreled 'about a woman.'

About three o'clock the two men met in the open space at the bridge entrance, which the Herald placed at the corner of Third Street and Washington Avenue in the business center. In the wire version Guffin drew a knife and Edwards fired four times, striking Guffin in the stomach and an elderly passer-by, Mrs. Garrity, in the shoulder. The Herald counted five shots and said the wounded were Mrs. Gassity and a man named Green, who was hit in the abdomen and was expected to die.

An 'immense crowd' gathered and the cry 'Lynch him' went up. Edwards, his pistol empty, was held while others ran for a rope, and the Herald wrote that 'in half a minute more he would have been dangling from a lamp post.' Four policemen then took him from the crowd and brought him to the police station, where he was locked up.

The Appeal called Guffin's wound mortal, and the Richmond Daily Palladium reported that Edwards had 'shot and killed' him. No later report of a death, an inquest, a charge against Edwards or any action against members of the crowd appears in the coverage.

White papers treated the episode as a sensational street shooting, with the near-lynching as its climax. The Dallas Daily Herald ran its special under the heading 'An Exciting Shooting Affair' and called Edwards 'the shootist,' while the Memphis Daily Appeal headed the wire 'Came Near Getting His Work In in St. Louis Yesterday.' The crowd appeared as 'enraged citizens' or 'an enraged mob,' and the Palladium credited Edwards's escape to 'the strenuous exertions of the police,' without further comment on the crowd.

Shorter versions ran in the Richmond Palladium and the St. Paul Daily Globe on September 14, the Globe's version naming Edwards and Griffin only as negroes and leaving out the steamer and the knife. A week later the same rewritten paragraph, dating the shooting 'on the 13th inst.,' appeared in crime roundups in the Mower County Transcript and the Watertown Republican on September 21 and the Superior Times on September 24.

The accounts differ on the date, the number of shots and who was hit. The Appeal's dateline reads September 12, but its text says 'this afternoon,' and the other dailies' 'yesterday' on September 14 and the Herald's September 13 dateline point to the 13th. Only the Herald names a wounded man called Green, and only the Palladium states that Guffin died.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Joe Edwards
bases: After Edwards shot at another Black man and wounded a passer-by, a street crowd seized him and sent for a rope to hang him, but police rescued him (A1, A2, A4): an attempted lynching.
A crowd held Edwards while men went for a rope and 'attempted to lynch' him (A1, A2), but police rescued him and took him to the station (A2, A3, A4); no one was killed by the crowd.
The Dallas Herald's own St. Louis special (A1) and the separate wire dispatch (A2, A3, A4) agree that a crowd tried to lynch Edwards after the shooting and that police saved him.

accounts.label: Dallas Herald St. Louis special
accounts.gist: A quarrel about a woman led Edwards to fire five times at Griffin, hitting Mrs. Gassity and a man named Green; the crowd held him and sent for a rope, and police came just in time.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Edwards and Guffin renewed a morning difficulty at the bridge entrance; Guffin drew a knife, Edwards fired four times, mortally wounding Guffin and hitting Mrs. Garrity; a crowd tried to lynch Edwards on the spot until four policemen rescued him.

framing.detail: The Herald headed its special 'An Exciting Shooting Affair' and wrote that Edwards would have been 'dangling from a lamp post' but for the police, without comment on the crowd.
Memphis, Richmond and St. Paul dailies ran the wire as a brief, the Appeal under 'Came Near Getting His Work In in St. Louis Yesterday'; the crowd is 'enraged citizens' or 'an enraged mob'.
Midwestern weeklies carried the story in a crime roundup a week or more later.

conflicts.note: A2's dateline says Sept. 12 but its text says 'this afternoon' and it ran on Sept. 14 with other Sept. 13 dispatches; the other dailies' 'yesterday' and A1's Sept. 13 dateline favor the 13th.

record_check.record: Edwards shot A. L. Grimm ... Grimm and two bystanders were wounded
record_check.dossier: The man Edwards shot at is Al Guffin / Griffin / Gaffin; the wounded named are Guffin (wire), Mrs. Garrity, and in one account a man named Green. No 'Grimm' appears.
Edwards was seized by the crowd at the scene before police arrived; he was not in custody when the crowd took hold of him.
A street crowd or mob, not a posse.
Seizure and threat (held while a rope was fetched); no pursuit is reported.
Only the Richmond Palladium says Guffin was killed; others say mortally wounded or that Green would probably die. No death is confirmed in the coverage, and none was caused by the crowd.
Supported; one dispatch's Sept. 12 dateline is likely an error.

info: Afternoon of September 13, 1881 (A1 'to-day' under a Sept. 13 dateline; A3, A4 'yesterday' on Sept. 14; A7 'the 13th inst.'); A2's dateline reads September 12.
Corner of Third Street and Washington Avenue (A1), described in the wire as 'the broad, open space at the bridge entrance' (A2, A3), in St. Louis's business center (A1).
Joe Edwards, described as 'colored' and 'negro', one of two 'negro firemen on the steamer Porter'.
Accused of shooting at Al Guffin (also Griffin, Gaffin), also Black, after a quarrel, wounding Guffin (A2, A3) or a man named Green (A1), and wounding a passing woman, Mrs. Garrity (Gassity).
A street crowd: 'an immense crowd' (A1), 'a crowd of enraged citizens' (A2), 'an enraged mob' (A4); no names or race given.
Edwards survived in police custody; no later report of his fate, an inquest or a trial was found.
